Where’s Waldo?
Query-language Preference under
Cross-lingual Knowledge Disparities

Dayeon Ki · Ruochen Zhang · Silviu Cucerzan
Ryen W. White · Ning Gao

University of Maryland · Microsoft

Preprint · September 2026

Kai Gu · Bocconi University
Reading group · 13 November 2026

Suppose I ask an AI a question in English, and you ask the same question in Chinese. We give it exactly the same evidence. Should the facts in our answers change?

This paper shows why the answer depends on whether a source is missing information or contradicting another source. I’ll introduce that comparison, then spend most of our time on the questions it opens for multilingual search and consumer decisions. The title gives us a useful way into the problem.

The paper

What’s Where’s Waldo?

Find one distinctive person
in a crowded scene.

Red-and-white stripes.
Glasses. A matching hat.

The paper’s version:
find the relevant fact
across languages.

WALDO = WikipediA Lost in
Disparity of knOwledge

Where’s Waldo? illustration: Martin Handford · supplied example

Where’s Waldo is a visual-search puzzle: the task is to find the striped character among many distracting people and objects. In this example, he is already circled, so we can see what the search is trying to recover.

The analogy is useful but incomplete. Finding a fact hidden in another language resembles finding Waldo. When two documents offer different answers, the task becomes deciding which account to follow. The paper studies that second difficulty as well as the first.

This collaboration connects multilingual NLP with information access. Ki’s work focuses on how people interpret AI across languages and cultures. Zhang studies multilingual representations, while White and Gao work on search, knowledge, and applied AI systems.

That combination helps explain the paper’s focus: the issue is not just whether a model can translate. It is whether a multilingual information system uses evidence consistently. The author links give additional background; the benchmark design makes that distinction concrete.

Design

Knowledge gaps and conflicts

Ki et al. (2026), Figure 1

Gap
Korean: after 2025.
English: fact absent.

Conflict
Korean: after 2025.
English: after 2023
(injected by the authors).

Comparison
Same two documents.
Change the query language.

≈12K QA pairs · 5 source languages + English · 8 models

In the example, the Korean article reports departure after the 2025 season. First, English has no such fact: that is a knowledge gap. Next, the authors insert a competing claim, departure after 2023, into English. That is a constructed knowledge conflict.

Each model sees both documents. The comparison changes the query language while holding the evidence fixed. Facts must postdate that model’s cutoff and fail a no-document answer check. This makes evidence use easier to isolate, but means the models are tested on different samples.

Read agreement as recovery of the original fact, not agreement between documents. In the top row, closed-model gaps are relatively small. Under conflict, they are large for every model. The bars show 95 percent bootstrap intervals; probability is a separate token-likelihood measure available only for open models.

The OpenAI pattern is descriptive because samples differ. Now imagine asking in English with English and Chinese documents supplied: the model sometimes accepts the Chinese account. GPT-5.5 does this in roughly 20 percent of conflict cases across source languages. What distinguishes those questions from the other 80 percent—local relevance or international scope? We can ask the same question in reverse without assuming the same rate.

Discussion · 1

Reversing the direction

Would naturally English-origin knowledge travel equally well into other languages?

Already tested

Swap original and conflicting facts across document languages.

Preference reverses direction.

Still open

Sample facts naturally present only in English.

Compare both directions on matched topics and source quality.

Paper: §5, Table 2 · proposed extension: natural English-origin gaps

The first direction question needs a qualification: the authors already reverse the conflict roles. They put the original fact in English and the conflicting version in the other language. Preference still follows the query language, with the sign reversed.

But translating and swapping the same facts does not reproduce the information ecosystem for naturally English-origin knowledge. English-only sources may cover different topics or carry different authority signals. I would compare both directions on matched topics before expecting the same magnitudes, especially for missing facts.

Discussion · 2

Beyond recent facts

Does the pattern survive when the task is interpreting evidence rather than retrieving a fact?

The benchmark targets discrete facts that postdate each model’s cutoff.

Factual question

“When did the coach leave?”

A date can match a reference.

Interpretive question

“Why did the coach leave?”

Competing explanations may each have support.

Proposed evaluation: evidence coverage, reasoning quality, and omissions.

A revision is not automatically about a recent event. Here, the authors go further: they retain facts whose event timestamp postdates the model’s cutoff. That intentionally reduces reliance on memorized knowledge and favors recent, discrete updates.

My interest is what changes when the user asks why. Different language communities may emphasize different explanations without disagreeing about the date. A reference-answer match becomes less informative. We would need to evaluate whether the explanation covers the available evidence and whether language systematically changes which reasons are omitted.

Discussion · 3

Genuinely contested knowledge

What should count as a good answer when the sources disagree for defensible reasons?

In WALDO

The researcher knows which fact was injected.

The original fact supplies the reference answer.

In a contested claim

Definitions, interests, or evidence may differ.

One reference answer may erase that disagreement.

Proposed test: preserve provenance, distinguish claims, express uncertainty.

The conflict task has a useful ground truth because the researchers know which statement they changed. That is different from a disagreement over causes, responsibility, or the meaning of an event. Neither source necessarily has a single demonstrably correct account.

In that setting, language-invariant answers could still be poor answers if they consistently suppress one perspective. I would reward the system for separating the claims, showing their support, and conveying what remains unresolved. This extends the benchmark from selecting a fact to representing a dispute.

Discussion · 4

From documents to AI search

How much of the language effect comes from which sources enter the answer context?

Main design: two supplied documents isolate evidence use.

Retrieval check: 100 QA pairs; four web documents added;
the original Wikipedia pair remains in every context.

Open-search extension: allow retrieval to omit either source;
separate retrieval, ranking, answer content, and citation choice.

Appendix B.1, pp. 26–27 · six-document robustness check

Supplying documents makes sense for isolating generation, but it may give the selected pair more influence than they would have in a real search. The paper does include retrieval: 100 questions, four added web documents, six documents total. The conflict pattern persists.

Crucially, the original pair is still guaranteed to appear, and the added languages are balanced by design. An open-search study should allow a source never to be retrieved. Then we can separate language effects in retrieval and ranking from effects in using and citing the evidence that survives.

Discussion · 5

Which questions cross languages?

What distinguishes the roughly 20% of questions where an English query follows the other-language account from the other 80%?

Local or international? Compare topics tied to the source-language context with topics of broader international relevance.

Test both directions: English query → Chinese account;
Chinese query → English account. Do the same topics cross over?

Compare question characteristics and cited sources across the two groups.

≈20%: GPT-5.5, pooled source languages · Chinese is an example.
Appendix C.4 tests locality in language gaps for open models; this comparison remains open.

My question is about which questions cross the language boundary. With both English and Chinese documents supplied, an English query sometimes leads the model to accept the Chinese account. Are those questions especially local to China, or do they concern international topics?

Compare their characteristics with the other 80 percent, then ask the same question in reverse. The roughly 20 percent is pooled across source languages, not a Chinese-specific or symmetric rate. The appendix tests locality in language gaps for open models; our proposed comparison concerns the questions behind these choices.

Discussion · 6

Where would it matter most?

Could language spillover improve discovery while language preference distorts a cross-border purchase?

Proposed setting: a Chinese-speaking shopper comparing
an imported product across local and English sources.

Language spillover

An English-only safety notice becomes accessible in Chinese.

Language preference

When sources conflict, query language changes the account used.

Measure verified accuracy, brand trust, purchase choice, and publisher traffic.

Here is a niche consumer setting where the two phenomena could have very different consequences. Imagine a shopper researching an imported product. An English-only safety notice could become accessible through a Chinese answer: that is a potential benefit of language spillover.

Now suppose local product pages conflict with the notice. Query-language preference could change the shopper’s perceived risk or purchase decision. This is a proposed study, not a finding here. We would verify the product version, market, and dates so genuine regional differences are not mislabeled as errors.

Discussion · 7

Do the same questions cross over?

Is the roughly 20% recovery stable across questions, or variable across repeated answers?

Stable selection

A subset of questions repeatedly favors the source-supported fact.

Candidate predictors: locality, authority, and clarity.

Sampling variation

The same question switches accounts across repeated runs.

Candidate predictors: decoding and weak evidence margins.

Repeat identical prompts; retain answer content and citations separately.

The roughly one-fifth English-query recovery for GPT-5.5 is an aggregate across questions. It does not tell us whether every question has a one-fifth chance of following the source account. A stable subset could account for most of those responses.

To distinguish the two stories, repeat identical prompts at fixed settings and compare variation within questions with variation across questions. Then relate stable choices to locality and source quality. Record citations separately: a citation can be inconsistent with the answer’s content, so neither measure should substitute for the other.

Discussion · 8

Comparing model generations

Would the opposing OpenAI patterns remain on exactly the same questions?

Observed: GPT-4o → GPT-4.1 → GPT-5.5
gap Δ: 5.5 → 3.5 → 0.3 pp · conflict Δ: 50.7 → 51.4 → 68.3 pp

Sample changes: 5,129 → 3,708 → 968 eligible QA pairs.

Use a common eligible sample, matched prompts and decoding,
and item-level paired comparisons with uncertainty.

Figure 2; Appendix A.5, Table 8 · descriptive comparison

The opposing OpenAI patterns are interesting enough to motivate a direct test. But the comparison combines model changes with sample changes. The eligible sample shrinks from 5,129 to 3,708 to 968 QA pairs because cutoffs and no-context performance differ.

I would evaluate a shared eligible set and report source-query and English-query recovery separately, not just their difference. A larger conflict gap can arise because source-query performance improves faster. That is a more precise interpretation than simply saying the newer model has become more biased.

Discussion · 9

What should we optimize?

Should a multilingual system give the same answer, the best-supported answer, or an explicit account of disagreement?

Consistency: the answer does not change with query language.

Accuracy: the answer follows the best-supported evidence.

Calibrated disagreement: unresolved conflicts remain visible.

Cross-language access is useful.
Conflict handling determines what that access delivers.

Discussion prompted by §6 mitigation and Appendix E, Prompt A.7

The paper also shows that head ablation and targeted fine-tuning can reduce the preference gap. But a smaller gap is not a complete definition of success. Two languages could receive the same incorrect answer, or the same overly confident treatment of an unresolved dispute.

The benchmark requests a single-sentence answer and one relevant document citation. I would compare that format with an option to acknowledge disagreement and cite both sources. Our closing question is therefore about the objective: when language changes access to evidence, what response best helps the user make a sound decision?
